sources.title: Beowulf
sources.author: Anonymous
sources.excerpt: Lo! We have heard of the glory of the Spear-Danes in days of yore, how the princes did deeds of prowess. How Scyld Scefing oft from the hosts of foes, from many tribes, bore away the mead-benches.
sources.longExcerpt:
Listen! We have heard of the glory of the Spear-Danes in days of yore, how those princes did deeds of prowess. How Scyld Scefing oft from the hosts of foes, from many tribes, bore away the mead-benches, struck terror into earls, after he first was found helpless (he met consolation for that); he grew under the heavens, throve in honors, until each of the neighboring peoples over the whale-road had to obey him, give him tribute. That was a good king!

To him was born a son, young in the yards, whom God sent to the people for a comfort. He perceived the dire distress that they suffered before, leaderless for a long while. The Lord of Life, the Ruler of Glory, gave him worldly honor. Beowulf was renowned - the fame of the son of Scyld spread wide in Danish lands.

Thus should a young man do good deeds, with generous gifts in his father's house, so that later in life loyal companions will stand by him when war comes, the people will serve him. Through praiseworthy deeds a man shall prosper among all peoples.

Then at the fated time Scyld departed, very strong, to go into the Lord's keeping. They bore him then to the sea's surf, his dear companions, as he himself had bidden while the friend of the Scyldings wielded words, the beloved land-ruler had ruled long. There in the harbor stood the ring-prowed ship, icy and eager to set out, the prince's vessel. Then they laid the beloved ruler, the giver of rings, in the bosom of the ship, the mighty one by the mast.

There was much treasure, ornaments from far-off lands were brought there. I have not heard of a ship more splendidly equipped with war-weapons and battle-dress, swords and mail-coats. On his bosom lay many treasures that were to travel far with him into the possession of the flood. They provided him with no lesser gifts, treasures of the people, than those had done who at his beginning first sent him forth alone over the waves, a child.

Then they set a golden standard high over his head, let the wave bear him, gave him to the ocean. Their hearts were sad, their spirits mournful. Men cannot truthfully say, neither counselors in hall nor heroes under the heavens, who received that cargo.

sources.title: Domesday Book
sources.author: William the Conqueror's officials
sources.excerpt: In the land of the King in Berkshire, the King holds Windsor. Earl Harold held it. There are 22 hides. There is land for 26 ploughs.
sources.longExcerpt:
The Domesday Book, commissioned by William the Conqueror in 1085, stands as one of the most remarkable administrative documents in European history. This great survey recorded the wealth and resources of England for taxation purposes.

In the twentieth year of his reign, by the grace of God, King William commanded that a survey be made of all England; of the lands in each of the counties; of the possessions of each of the magnates, their lands, their households, their men both bond and free, living in huts or with their own houses and lands; of plows, horses, and other animals; of the services and payments due from each and every estate.

Berkshire: In the land of the King in Berkshire, the King holds Windsor. Earl Harold held it. There are 22 hides. There is land for 26 ploughs. In demesne are 5 ploughs; and 22 villeins and 2 bordars with 20 ploughs. There is a priest with 1 hide, and 2 knights with 3 hides. There are 2 mills rendering 15 shillings, and 110 acres of meadow. Woodland for 50 pigs, and from the wood and grazing, 10 shillings. In the time of King Edward it was worth 15 pounds; now it is worth 15 pounds.

The manor of Reading: The King holds Reading. Earl Harold held it. There are 43 hides. There is land for 40 ploughs. In demesne are 4 hides, and there are 4 ploughs. There are 55 villeins and 30 bordars with 38 ploughs. There is a church, and 8 slaves, and 4 mills rendering 35 shillings, and 2 fisheries rendering 10 shillings, and 105 acres of meadow. Woodland for 80 pigs.

So thorough was this survey that it was said that not an ox, nor a cow, nor a pig escaped notice. The English people called it the Domesday Book because, like the Day of Judgment, its decisions were final and could not be appealed. The survey covered all of England except the northern counties, which were still recovering from William's harrying of the North.

The book remains an invaluable source for understanding medieval England, providing detailed information about land ownership, resources, and social structure in the late 11th century.

sources.title: The Song of Roland
sources.author: Anonymous
sources.excerpt: Roland is brave and Oliver is wise, and both for valor may bear away the prize. Death they will die ere they be recreant.
sources.longExcerpt:
The Song of Roland, the oldest surviving major work of French literature, recounts the heroic deeds of Charlemagne's nephew Roland at the Battle of Roncevaux Pass in 778.

Charles the King, our great Emperor, has been in Spain for seven full years, and has conquered the proud land as far as the sea. Not a castle remains that stands against him; not a wall or city is left to destroy, except Saragossa, which stands on a mountain. King Marsile holds it, who does not love God, but serves Mohammed and prays to Apollo. Yet he cannot prevent disaster from reaching him there.

King Marsile was in Saragossa. He has gone into an orchard, under the shade. He lies down on a block of blue marble, with more than twenty thousand men around him. He calls his dukes and his counts: 'Hear, lords, what disaster weighs upon us. The Emperor Charles of sweet France has come to this country to destroy us.'

Count Roland rides through the battlefield, holding Durendal, which cuts and slashes well. He has brought great slaughter upon the Saracens. If you could see him piling corpse upon corpse, and the clear blood spreading in pools! His hauberk is all bloodied, and his arms, and his good horse's neck and shoulders.

Roland is brave and Oliver is wise, and both for valor may bear away the prize. Once they are armed and mounted on their horses, not even for death would they avoid a battle. The counts are worthy men, and their words are fierce. The pagans ride in great fury.

Oliver says: 'Roland, see all these pagans! They are very close to us, but Charles is too far away. You did not deign to sound your horn. If the king were here, we would suffer no harm. Look toward the Spanish passes - you can see, the rearguard is pitiful. Whoever is part of this one will never be part of another.'

Roland answers: 'Do not speak such folly! Cursed be the heart that turns coward in the chest! We shall stand our ground firmly in this place, and here we shall provide the blows and the combat.'

sources.title: Magna Carta
sources.author: English Barons
sources.excerpt: No free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions, or outlawed or exiled, except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land.
sources.longExcerpt:
John, by the grace of God King of England, Lord of Ireland, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou, to his archbishops, bishops, abbots, earls, barons, justices, foresters, sheriffs, stewards, servants, and to all his officials and loyal subjects, Greeting.

Know that before God, for the health of our soul and those of our ancestors and heirs, to the honor of God, the exaltation of the holy Church, and the better ordering of our kingdom, at the advice of our reverend fathers Stephen, archbishop of Canterbury, primate of all England, and cardinal of the holy Roman Church, Henry archbishop of Dublin, and the noble men William Marshal earl of Pembroke, William earl of Salisbury, and others:

First, that we have granted to God, and by this present charter have confirmed for us and our heirs in perpetuity, that the English Church shall be free, and shall have its rights undiminished, and its liberties unimpaired.

We have also granted to all free men of our realm, for us and our heirs forever, all the underwritten liberties, to be had and held by them and their heirs, of us and our heirs:

No free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions, or outlawed or exiled, or deprived of his standing in any way, nor will we proceed with force against him, or send others to do so, except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land.

To no one will we sell, to no one deny or delay right or justice.

All merchants shall have safe and secure exit from England, and entry to England, with the right to tarry there and to move about as well by land as by water, for buying and selling by the ancient and right customs, quit from all evil tolls, except in time of war.

Given by our hand in the meadow that is called Runnymede, between Windsor and Staines, on the fifteenth day of June in the seventeenth year of our reign.

sources.author: Anna Komnenos
sources.excerpt: The Frankish counts are naturally shameless and violent, naturally greedy of money too, and immoderate in everything they wish, and possess a flow of language greater than any other human race. They did not make their visits to the emperor in any order.
